They differ in whether conflicting/stale information is actively removed. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an indexing/retrieval framework: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph (OpenIE triples plus synonym and passage nodes) and retrieves via Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. It has no mechanism for handling new or conflicting information—new passages are simply added to the graph, and nothing excises superseded states; the pages describe no update/conflict-resolution procedure [2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s11.p1]. GC-Mem, by contrast, is an inference-time consistency protocol aimed exactly at this: it formalizes Semantic Shadowing, where an updated entity's old state is not deleted and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale contradictory chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. GC-Mem applies a temporal dominance operator Φ_T with a pairwise NLI contradiction detector over the retrieved candidate set, excising any older chunk contradicted by a newer one, so that if a valid chunk is retrieved P(y=S_new)→1 [2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. It is bounded by detector recall (>50% needed) and adds O(k²) cost [2609.16073#s20.p1][2609.16073#s20.p2]. In short: HippoRAG accumulates and associates without conflict handling, while GC-Mem prunes temporally dominated conflicting memories at query time [2609.16073#s1.p1].

respuesta:
HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) has no explicit mechanism for handling new or conflicting information: it is an append-only indexing scheme. Offline, an LLM extracts OpenIE triples from each passage and builds a knowledge graph with synonym edges and passage nodes [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]; new passages are simply added to this graph, and retrieval runs Personalized PageRank over it [2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s11.p1]. Nothing in the design detects contradictions, overwrites, or invalidates older facts — so when a fact is updated, the stale and new versions coexist and compete. Empirically this shows: on FactConsolidation, HippoRAG-v2 reaches 54.0 single-hop but only 5.0 multi-hop accuracy [2507.05257#s21.p3], and it is cited as a baseline that fails at selective forgetting/overwriting [2507.05257#s48.p1].

GC-Mem instead treats conflicting information explicitly at inference time. It keeps the store append-only but runs a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies a temporal dominance operator Φ_T, excising any older chunk contradicted by a newer one, so that if a valid chunk is retrieved all older contradictory chunks are removed and P(y=S_new)→1 [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. This targets 'semantic shadowing', where stale and updated states are semantically equivalent and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. On its Temporal Mutation Benchmark GC-Mem reaches 97.3% CR-Acc on deepseek-v3 Large versus 56.8% for Standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3], though it requires a detector with >50% recall [2609.16073#s20.p1].

In short: HippoRAG accumulates new knowledge into a graph index without resolving conflicts, whereas GC-Mem detects contradictions among retrieved chunks and prunes the temporally dominated (older) ones [2609.16073#s1.p1][2609.16073#s9.p4].

respuesta: They differ in where and how conflicts are resolved. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an append-only indexing/retrieval framework: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph with synonym and passage edges and retrieves via Personalized PageRank, with no mechanism for rewriting, invalidating, or superseding existing memories when new or contradictory information arrives [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Consequently it handles conflicting facts poorly: on FactConsolidation it reaches only 54.0 single-hop and 5.0 multi-hop accuracy, versus 62.7/8.8 for ReFind, whose gains are attributed to chronology- and session-aware controls that distinguish the relevant version of a fact [2507.05257#s21.p3][2608.12888#s23.p3][2608.12888#s24.p2]. GC-Mem instead targets exactly this problem: it keeps the store append-only but, at inference time, runs a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies a temporal dominance operator that excises older contradictory chunks, so if any valid chunk is retrieved P(y=S_new)→1 [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. This lifts Conflict Resolution Accuracy to 97.3% on deepseek-v3 Large versus 56.8% for Standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3], though it depends on a detector with >50% recall and adds O(k²) cost [2609.16073#s20.p1][2609.16073#s20.p2]. In short: HippoRAG leaves new/conflicting information to accumulate and relies on retrieval, while GC-Mem actively detects contradictions and prunes temporally dominated (stale) context at query time [2609.16073#s1.p1][2609.16073#s9.p4].

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG memory update new information consolidation

respuesta: HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) has no explicit mechanism for handling new or conflicting information: it is an offline indexing + retrieval framework that builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph and retrieves via Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4]. New passages are simply indexed into the graph, and conflicts are left to the reader/context — on FactConsolidation, HippoRAG-v2 reaches only 54.0 single-hop and 5.0 multi-hop accuracy, i.e. it largely fails to overwrite outdated facts [2507.05257#s21.p3]. GC-Mem instead handles conflicts at retrieval time: it keeps the store append-only but excises contradicted older chunks from the retrieved context via temporal dominance [2609.16073#s9.p4], reaching 97.3% Conflict Resolution Accuracy on deepseek-v3 Large versus 56.8% for Standard RAG [2609.16073#s14.p3]. So HippoRAG relies on graph indexing without conflict resolution, while GC-Mem actively filters stale/contradicted chunks during retrieval.

HaluMem (HaluMem: Evaluating Hallucinations in Memory Systems of Agents) is the operation-level benchmark that checks whether a memory system invents false facts during memory extraction, memory updating, and memory question answering [2511.03506#s1.p1][2511.03506#s5.p6]. It supplies stage-specific gold standards—an extraction set, update pairs, and per-query answers—and scores each stage separately rather than treating the system as a black box [2511.03506#s6.p8]. Its metrics include False Memory Resistance (fraction of injected distractors ignored) for extraction, plus hallucination rates for updating and QA [2511.03506#s12.p2][2511.03506#s14.p6][2511.03506#s15.p5].

pasos.argumento: memory system hallucination false facts benchmark

respuesta: HaluMem is the benchmark: it is the first operation-level hallucination evaluation benchmark for memory systems, scoring hallucinations at memory extraction, memory updating, and memory QA with stage-specific gold standards [2511.03506#s1.p1][2511.03506#s6.p8]. Its updating and QA metrics explicitly include hallucination rates (alongside accuracy and omission) [2511.03506#s14.p6][2511.03506#s15.p5], and extraction includes False Memory Resistance against injected distractors [2511.03506#s12.p2].

The two differ fundamentally: WikiLoop explicitly trains its knowledge base using downstream feedback, while HippoRAG 2's knowledge graph is built offline with no downstream signal.

WikiLoop — feedback-coupled construction. WikiLoop couples construction of an agent-native Wiki to the downstream agent that consumes it within a single role-conditioned policy [2607.26604#s1.p1]. It identifies that construction usually "receives no signal from downstream use" as the core problem [2607.26604#s1.p1]. The Builder's reward is the marginal change in navigation utility: each rollout applies one patch to an isolated copy and runs a frozen Navigator on both states, giving ΔU_affected and ΔU_guard [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p12]. The reward is ΔU_affected minus a one-sided guard penalty, edit cost, and structure penalty [2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s7.p17]. This marginal-utility credit is needed because absolute post-edit performance confounds edit quality with the pre-edit Wiki's quality [2607.26604#s2.p3]. The guard term cuts Guard Regression from 0.046 to 0.016 while held-out ΔU rises from 0.077 to 0.084 [2607.26604#s12.p12].

HippoRAG 2 — no downstream feedback loop. HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph offline: an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples, synonym edges are added by embedding similarity, and passages become nodes linked by "contains" edges [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Online, an LLM filter keeps only relevant triples as seeds for Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. The LLM is used at query time for filtering, but the graph structure itself is never revised by downstream answer quality — there is no reward or credit-assignment mechanism tied to retrieval outcomes. Its improvements come from architectural choices (query-to-triple matching, passage nodes, filtering), validated by ablations rather than learned from feedback [2502.14802#s19.p1][2502.14802#s17.p5].

In short, WikiLoop treats the knowledge base as a policy trained against downstream navigation utility with guarded marginal-utility credit [2607.26604#s7.p14], whereas HippoRAG 2 treats it as a fixed offline index whose only downstream LLM use is query-time triple filtering [2502.14802#s10.p1].

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG 2 downstream feedback knowledge base

respuesta:
They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. HippoRAG 2 (and HippoRAG) builds its knowledge graph/index with off-the-shelf components and no fine-tuning: OpenIE triples, synonymy edges, and Personalized PageRank retrieval are all used as-is, with no signal from downstream QA performance feeding back into construction [2405.14831#s21.p2][2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4]. Its improvements come from the indexing/retrieval design, not from learning against the consumer.

WikiLoop instead explicitly couples construction to the downstream consumer: a single role-conditioned policy both builds and navigates an agent-native Wiki, and the Builder is trained on downstream navigation utility [2607.26604#s1.p1]. Each candidate edit is scored by the before/after utility difference under a frozen Navigator (ΔU_affected minus a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on guard queries, plus edit-cost and structure penalties), with GRPO/GSPO advantages [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s8.p11]. This is an instance of downstream-reward training (RLGF-style), where the reward is derived from final answer quality rather than intermediate labels [2607.26604#s7.p8].

In short: HippoRAG 2 optimizes a fixed, off-the-shelf graph index with no downstream feedback loop, whereas WikiLoop learns the knowledge-base construction itself from downstream navigation/answer utility, with guarded marginal-utility credit for each edit [2607.26604#s1.p1][2607.26604#s7.p14].

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG 2 downstream feedback training knowledge base construction

respuesta:
They differ fundamentally: WikiLoop uses downstream feedback to train its knowledge-base builder, while HippoRAG 2 does not use downstream feedback at all for construction.

WikiLoop: construction and navigation are coupled in one role-conditioned policy, and the Builder is trained on downstream navigation utility. Each candidate patch is applied to an isolated Wiki copy and scored by the before/after utility difference under a frozen Navigator, with a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s7.p17]. Freezing the Navigator keeps the utility scale stationary [2607.26604#s7.p18]. This yields large gains: unguarded ΔU raises affected ΔAC to 12.8, and the guard term cuts Guard Regression from 0.046 to 0.016 [2607.26604#s12.p11][2607.26604#s12.p12].

HippoRAG 2: its knowledge graph is built offline by LLM OpenIE triple extraction plus synonym and passage/context edges, and retrieval uses query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. Nothing in its construction is optimized against downstream answer quality; its improvements come from architectural design (passage nodes, filtering, query-to-triple), validated by ablations rather than feedback-driven training [2502.14802#s19.p1][2502.14802#s17.p5].

In short, WikiLoop closes the loop between KB construction and its consumer via RL on downstream utility, whereas HippoRAG 2 builds a fixed graph index with no downstream-feedback signal into construction.

pasos.argumento: HippoRAG 2 downstream feedback knowledge base construction

respuesta: They differ in whether downstream feedback is used at all. HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph offline with an LLM (OpenIE triples, synonym edges, passage nodes) and retrieves with query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, and Personalized PageRank; its construction is not trained or refined by any downstream answer-quality signal — the LLM filter acts only at query time on retrieved triples [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. WikiLoop instead couples construction to the downstream consumer: a Builder is trained with RL on the marginal change in downstream navigation utility caused by each edit, measured by running a frozen Navigator on isolated before/after Wiki states, with a one-sided guard penalty for regressions on unrelated queries [2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p9][2607.26604#s7.p14][2607.26604#s7.p17]. This guarded marginal-utility credit reduces Guard Regression from 0.046 to 0.016 while keeping affected ΔAC at 12.1 [2607.26604#s12.p12], and the shared role-conditioned policy yields 62.6 All AC versus 55.8 for HippoRAG 2 [2607.26604#s11.p3][2607.26604#s11.p4]. In short, HippoRAG 2's structured index is fixed after offline extraction, whereas WikiLoop optimizes its structured Wiki directly against downstream feedback [2607.26604#s1.p1].
